title: Hot-window fragmentation — multi-workload surge diary
content:
Purpose / context
  -----------------
  Quick running diary of an investigation into a recurring tail-latency pattern we see when multiple tenants burst simultaneously (usually after cron jobs, short background batch updates, or synchronous A/B tests). Hypothesis: the resident KV working set becomes fragmented at page boundaries during surges which increases NVMe read-amplification and causes DMA stalls on memory channels, amplifying per-token tail latencies even when overall occupancy isn't high.

  Why this is different from previous kv-eviction work
  ---------------------------------------------------
  We have plenty of notes on eviction heuristics, TTLs, prefetch predictors, etc. This document focuses on the microstructure of the resident set: page-level fragmentation, cross-tenant interleaving, and how the NVMe/PCIe/DMA stack reacts during short high-concurrency bursts (0.5–10s). The measurable effect looks less like classic eviction thrash and more like short-lived read-amplification + channel backpressure.

  Observation summary (what we see in prod-like tests)
  ---------------------------------------------------
  - Case: 6 tenants, mixed seqlens (8/64/256). At steady-state latency p50/p95 stable; during a coordinated 20s burst latency p99 spikes 2.5–4x.
  - KV hit-rate drops only modestly (~5–8%), but NVMe IO per request spikes 30–60%.
  - BPFtrace and nvprof traces show increased DMA stall counts and longer DMA completion latencies coincident with the spike.
  - Hot keys remain mostly hot; the problem correlates with the emergence of many medium-frequency keys whose pages are resident but scattered across many pages (high fragmentation).
  - Prefetching (naive next-page) actually makes the spike worse in some tests because it floods DMA with small random reads.

  Testbed / repro steps (lab)
  ---------------------------
  Hardware:
  - 8x A100-like GPU worker; host: 2x 24-core AMD CPUs, 512GB RAM
  - NVMe pool: 4x high-qdepth SSDs, single NVMe namespace per host
  - Kernel: Ubuntu 22.04 + 6.2 with our custom io_uring patches

  Software/versions:
  - serving-runtime: commit d7a8c5a
  - kv store: resident pager v3.4 (page-granularity 2MB)
  - monitoring: bpftrace v0.13, perf 5.x, nvtop for card telemetry

  Repro script (short form):
  1) Populate resident set with 10M keys using mixed access distribution (zipf 0.9) and mark 35% as medium-frequency.
  2) Run steady-state generator (50 rps per tenant) until warm.
  3) Trigger simultaneous surge: 6 tenants => 500 rps each for 20s, then back to baseline.
  4) Collect per-request tracing (kv residency, page id list), host perf counters (dma_stalls, pci bandwidth), and nvme queue latencies.

  Key measurements collected
  --------------------------
  - Per-request page list sizes: median 1 page, p95 12 pages during surge
  - NVMe read amplification factor (reads_per_token): baseline 1.2 -> surge 1.9
  - DMA stall events (per-second): baseline 120 -> surge 420
  - PCIe utilization: small uptick but Q-depth saturation observed at tail
  - Swapback/prefetch thread CPU: increases, but mainly blocked on io completions

  Detailed traces (high level)
  ----------------------------
  - Trace A (tenant A, seq64): token 120–140 shows repeated per-token pause ~1.2ms correlated to NVMe completion waits. Page residency indicated many scattered page-ids for next-token KV reads.
  - Trace B (tenant D, seq8): unaffected p50 but p99 shows ~2ms jitter. Smaller reads but more frequent DMA pipeline stalls.

  Early hypotheses (cause chain)
  ------------------------------
  1) Multi-tenant bursts cause many medium-frequency keys to be touched in a short window.
  2) Those keys map to pages that are scattered (fragmentation) so the IO engine sees many small random reads across namespaces.
  3) NVMe and DMA engine have non-linear cost when handling many small concurrent reads (queue thrash, head-of-line blocking across channels) causing higher per-read latency.
  4) Cumulative effect: more CPU threads blocked, prefetch/workers queue up, KV request latencies amplify for tail tokens.

  Mitigation experiments run so far
  --------------------------------
  - Coalesced read batching in the pager: group page reads by page-id and issue single larger IOs where contiguous — result: reduced read amplification by ~18%, lowered p99 by ~12% in synthetic tests.
  - Adaptive micro-reservation: reserve adjacent pages when a medium-frequency key first accessed within a short window — result: good for some distributions, but increased false-warmth for others (raises steady-state IO slightly).
  - Smoothing ingress by soft admission (delay a subset of burst requests by 5–10ms): reduces DMA bursts and tails but impacts latency SLOs; operationally undesirable.
  - Prefetch backpressure: throttle prefetch worker concurrency during detected DMA saturation — promising effect on tail, avoids worst-case flooding.

  Negative results / things that didn't help
  -----------------------------------------
  - Increasing global KV cache size by 20% didn't eliminate spikes.
  - Simple LRU-chunk coalescing (merge small slots) reduced fragmentation metric but increased eviction churn and hurt tail in mixed workloads.
  - Naive next-page prefetch increased IO fanout and made peaks worse.

  Open questions
  --------------
  - Is NVMe firmware scheduling exacerbating Q-depth issues across multiple queues? Need vendor I/O trace.
  - How much of the fragmentation is allocator policy (our 2MB page mapping) vs. eviction pattern? Would using 1MB or 4MB change the tradeoff?
  - Can we encode cross-tenant locality hints (e.g., tenant-aware clustering) without violating multi-tenant isolation/policy?
  - Are there hardware knobs (PCIe weights, NVMe queue pairing) we can tune in prod?

  Next steps / immediate action items
  ----------------------------------
  - (Chris) File a vendor support trace request for NVMe queue behavior during bursts (INF-1842 is linked).
  - (Ravi) Prototype pager-level coalescer that groups non-contiguous page reads into a small number of larger IOs (limit 16 pages) and compare in mixed-tenant tests.
  - (Elena) Add a telemetry signal: per-request \"page-fragmentation-score\" (num_pages / expected_pages) and surface in Console heatmaps for the next sprint.
  - (Sofia) Run allocator sweep: test 1MB/2MB/4MB page mappings on staging to gather sensitivity curves.
  - Add canary experiment: enable prefetch-backpressure in 5% of hosts for 48h and monitor p99 and IO amplification.

  Notes-to-self / heuristics found
  --------------------------------
  - Fragmentation score >= 6 (p95 pages/request / median pages/request) correlates strongly with p99 spikes.
  - Combining coalescing + prefetch backpressure was more stable than either alone.
  - Document the synthetic workload used (zipf param, tenant mix) in Confluence page referenced above so others can reproduce.

  Rough conclusion
  ----------------
  We are looking at a fragmentation-driven read-amplification phenomenon that shows up strongly during short multi-tenant surges. The immediate wins are pager-level coalescing and backing off prefetch concurrency when DMA/backpressure signals appear. Longer-term fixes may require allocator tweaks or deeper NVMe/PCIe tuning. This is orthogonal to eviction-policy work; it sits between allocation and IO scheduling.

  Attachments / raw artifacts
  --------------------------
  - perf traces (raw) uploaded to the infra bucket: s3://redwood-infra/kv-frag-2025-10-15
  - BPFtrace scripts used: /repos/serving-runtime/tools/bpf/kv-frag.bt

  End diary entry. Will update with vendor feedback and staging allocator sweeps.
